newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Bhutto party sees extending presidential rule.
newsitem.headline: Bhutto party sees extending presidential rule.

text.p: Ousted prime minister Benazir Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party (PPP) accused President Farooq Leghari and his aides on Saturday of aiming to impose a presidential form of government, which it woved to oppose.
Its Central Executive Committee (CEC) also said Leghari had plunged Pakistan into "a state of limbo and uncertainty (and) constitutional and economic crises" by sacking Bhutto.

Leghari, a former Bhutto protege, sacked her three-year-old government on November 5 charging it with corruption and misrule, dissolved the lower house of parliament, and appointed a caretaker government to hold fresh elections on February 3.

A resolution passed by a CEC meeting in Islamabad, the first since Bhutto's dismissal, said Leghari's "accomplices" were trying to destroy Pakistan's parliamentary system of government and replace it with "one-man dictatorship and usurpation of all powers by the president".

The reference seemed aimed at current hearings of petitions by the Supreme Court on whether the prime minister's advice to the president on the appointment of judges of superior courts is mandatory or not.
"Any attempt to render the office of prime minister powerless and vest all executive powers in the president shall be opposed by the people," said the resolution issued at a news conference.
"Such an attempt would only negate the will of people, destroy the parliamentary form of democracy, erode the federal structure and usurp the autonomy enjoyed by provinces," it said.
"The CEC, therefore, warns the president to desist from carrying out such nefarious aims and designs which will seriously harm the federation."

The PPP has yet to decide whether it will take part in the February 3 vote and says that for the moment it will concentrate on Bhutto's petition to the Supreme Court seeking a reversal of her dismissal and restoration of her cabinet.

Saturday's meeting called the caretaker cabinet of Prime Minister Meraj Khalid a group of "friends, cronies and relatives (of the president) and disgruntled elements having prejudices against the PPP and its leadership".

It said the caretaker cabinet was "for decoration only" while the country was being run by what it called a troika of president, his principal secretary and his friend Shahid Hamid, who is minister for defence in Khalid's cabinet.
In an apparent move to end a row between Bhutto and her mother Nusrat over the party leadership, the committee named Nusrat to a newly created figurehead office of "Rahnuma (guiding) chairperson".
Bhutto had ousted her mother as PPP chairperson in December 1993 after Nusrat supported her son, Murtaza, in October elections against the PPP's official candidates.

Murtaza, who later formed a breakaway Shaheed Bhutto faction of the PPP, was killed by police last month in the port city of Karachi in a shootout that Bhutto called a conspiracy against her family and government.
Murtaza's Lebanese wife, Ghinwa, announced in Karachi on Saturday that she would lead her husband's faction and contest election from Bhutto's home town of Larkana in the southern province of Sindh.

Ghinawa, a former teacher who speaks English, French and her native Arabic, has taken Pakistani nationality. She is the first Arab woman to lead a Pakistani political group, although not the first foreign-born.
